lesson.title: Kubernetes from Zero, part 18: taints, priority and disruption budgets
lesson.description: Keep Pods off nodes with taints, let important Pods push others aside with PriorityClass, and drain a node safely behind a PodDisruptionBudget.
lesson.tested: Every command ran on a four-node kind v0.33.0 cluster (node v1.37.0, kubectl v1.37.2) on 10 Nov 2026
lesson.rule: Taint nodes to reserve them, give critical Pods a higher priority, and put a PodDisruptionBudget on every replicated app before anyone drains a node.

cheatsheet.intro: Taints, priority, drain, and the commands from Lesson 18.

rows.name: Taint
rows.role: Keeps Pods off a node. A toleration lets a Pod in and does not pull it there. NoExecute also evicts running Pods.

rows.name: PriorityClass
rows.role: Ranks Pods. When the cluster is full, a higher priority can preempt a lower one. No class means priority 0.

rows.name: PDB
rows.role: Limits voluntary disruption. Only tools that use the Eviction API, such as kubectl drain, respect it. kubectl delete pod does not.

rows.name: Maintenance
rows.role: Cordon, drain, work, uncordon. Pods that moved away do not come back on their own.

rows.name: dedicated=gpu
rows.role: NoSchedule on worker3. Six web replicas without a toleration stayed on the other two workers. trainer, with a toleration and a nodeSelector, ran on worker3.

rows.name: NoExecute
rows.role: impatient was evicted at once. patient, with tolerationSeconds 20, stayed and was gone by the later check.

rows.name: Preemption
rows.role: Six batch Pods at priority 1000 requested 3 CPU and left 1.9 CPU free. checkout at 100000 and 4 CPU preempted batch on worker3. The replacement stayed Pending with Insufficient cpu.

rows.name: Drain
rows.role: minAvailable 3 on 3 replicas showed ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS 0 and the drain could not evict. minAvailable 2 allowed the eviction.

items.what: The control-plane node already carries node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule, which is why ordinary Pods stay off it.
The event named batch-5bd8dd9495-mw2hl, preempted on k8s-ep16-worker3 so checkout could run there.
The refused drain said it would violate the pod's disruption budget. Lower the budget, or scale up. Do not delete the PDB in a hurry.
The lesson prefers maxUnavailable 1 over minAvailable N, because it still allows a disruption after a scale.

homework.intro: Use the three-worker kind cluster from part 17 and the namespace k8s-from-zero. The lesson's cluster is k8s-ep16. Answers are in the separate answer key.

sections.title: Recall
sections.hint: Answer from memory, then check the lesson.

exercises.q: What is the difference between a taint and a toleration?
exercises.a: A taint keeps Pods off a node. A toleration lets a Pod in. It does not attract the Pod. NoExecute also evicts running Pods that do not tolerate it, after tolerationSeconds if that is set.

exercises.q: Which disruptions does a PodDisruptionBudget limit?
exercises.a: Voluntary ones, and only when the tool uses the Eviction API. kubectl drain does. kubectl delete pod does not check the budget.

exercises.q: What priority does a Pod with no PriorityClass get, and what does preemptionPolicy Never do?
exercises.a: Priority 0. preemptionPolicy Never lets the Pod queue first without evicting others. The field is on the PriorityClass.

exercises.q: Taint worker3 with dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule and apply the web Deployment with no toleration. Where do the six replicas land?
exercises.a: On the other two workers only. The trainer Pod, which tolerates the taint and selects that node, runs on worker3.

exercises.q: Apply the batch Deployment and then checkout. What did the lesson record for CPU and for the preempted Pod?
exercises.a: Each worker showed cpu 6100m (76%) with 1.9 CPU free, not enough for checkout's 4 CPU request. batch-5bd8dd9495-mw2hl was preempted on worker3. The replacement stayed Pending with Insufficient cpu.

exercises.q: With minAvailable 3 and three web Pods, drain a worker with a 20 second timeout. What does get pdb show, and does the drain finish?
exercises.a: ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS is 0. The drain keeps failing because an eviction would violate the budget. After the patch to minAvailable 2, the eviction succeeds.

sections.title: Predict the outcome
sections.hint: Write your prediction first. Then check the answer key.

exercises.q: A node dies. How long do its Pods stay, according to the lesson?
exercises.a: Every Pod tolerates node.kubernetes.io/not-ready and node.kubernetes.io/unreachable with tolerationSeconds 300, so replacement waits about five minutes.

exercises.q: kubectl drain hangs on Cannot evict pod. What does the lesson tell you to check, and what should you not do?
exercises.a: kubectl get pdb -A. A row with ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS 0 blocks the drain. Scale the app up or lower minAvailable. Do not delete the PDB in a hurry on a production app.

exercises.q: You uncordon a node after a drain. Do the Pods that moved come back?
exercises.a: No. uncordon only allows new scheduling. Pods that moved away stay where they are.
